vulnerability.title: Netty SniHandler allocates a ClientHello-sized buffer from an unvalidated length, up to 16MB per connection

fixed_releases.verified_content: At 4.1.94.Final SslClientHelloHandler has MAX_CLIENT_HELLO_LENGTH=0xFFFFFF, a maxClientHelloLength field and constructors, and rejects handshakeLength > maxClientHelloLength with TooLongFrameException before allocating; SniHandler and AbstractSniHandler expose the limit through new constructors. The guard requires maxClientHelloLength != 0, and most default paths pass 0: AbstractSniHandler() calls this(0, 0L), SniHandler(Mapping) -> SniHandler(AsyncMapping) -> this(mapping, 0, 0L), and the handshake-timeout-only constructors delegate with 0 as well. The no-argument SslClientHelloHandler defaults to 0xFFFFFF, which getUnsignedMedium can never exceed. The mitigation therefore only takes effect when the application explicitly passes a maxClientHelloLength in [1, 0xFFFFFF].

vulnerability.category_l2: Unbounded allocation: the ClientHello handshake length (attacker-controlled 24-bit field) is used directly as ByteBuf capacity before the bytes arrive, so a short crafted record costs up to 16MB of heap per connection

description: Netty's SniHandler waits for the TLS ClientHello to select an SslContext, and inherits its record decoding from SslClientHelloHandler (SniHandler line 37 extends AbstractSniHandler, which line 32 extends SslClientHelloHandler). At 4.1.59 SslClientHelloHandler.decode reads the handshake length with in.getUnsignedMedium at lines 117-118; that is a 24-bit value controlled by the peer and can be as large as 0xFFFFFF (about 16MB). When the declared handshake does not fit in the current TLS record, lines 130-132 call ctx.alloc().buffer(handshakeLength) with that value and no upper bound, before any of those bytes have arrived, and line 141 copies the record payload into the buffer. A client can therefore send a small record whose declared handshake length is 0xFFFFFF and make the server hold a 16MB buffer per connection; repeating this on many connections, with no idle timeout to release them, exhausts the heap. The 4.1.94.Final fix 535da17e adds maxClientHelloLength and throws TooLongFrameException before the allocation when handshakeLength exceeds a configured limit, and exposes the limit through new SniHandler and AbstractSniHandler constructors. The protection is opt-in only: MAX_CLIENT_HELLO_LENGTH stays 0xFFFFFF (a value handshakeLength can never exceed) and the default AbstractSniHandler()/SniHandler(Mapping) paths pass maxClientHelloLength=0, which disables the check, so upgrading alone does not change the default allocation bound.

critical_operation.description: handshakeLength comes from in.getUnsignedMedium (lines 117-118), a three-byte field in the peer's ClientHello header, so it ranges up to 0xFFFFFF (16777215 bytes). The else branch at 130-132 allocates a ByteBuf of exactly that capacity when the ClientHello is split across records, with no maximum and before the payload is received. SniHandler inherits this decode unchanged. The fix inserts a maxClientHelloLength check at 4.1.94 lines 140-147 before this allocation and throws TooLongFrameException.

entry_point.description: A TCP server with SniHandler in its pipeline: SniHandler (line 37 extends AbstractSniHandler<SslContext>, itself extending SslClientHelloHandler) receives the inbound TLS records through the inherited ByteToMessageDecoder.decode callback.

source_crosscheck.notes: CNA, NVD, OSV and the GitHub advisory agree on the mechanism (SniHandler/SslClientHelloHandler allocates up to 16MB from the ClientHello-declared length), on the 6.5 Medium CVSS 3.1 vector and on the 4.1.94.Final fix. CWE differs by source but not by family: the CNA lists CWE-400, NVD lists CWE-770 as Primary with CWE-400 Secondary, and GHSA lists both. The patch and the 4.1.94 source confirm the fix adds a configurable maximum and a TooLongFrameException check; the independent reviewer established that the default maximum is not effectively lowered (0xFFFFFF cannot be exceeded and the default constructor paths pass 0, which disables the check), so the mitigation is opt-in and this is recorded as a limitation. This root cause is distinct from the previously promoted netty entries: CVE-2021-37136 (Bzip2 decompression resource use), CVE-2021-37137 (Snappy frame decoder resource use), CVE-2021-43797 (CRLF injection in header validation), CVE-2021-21295 (HTTP/2 request smuggling) and CVE-2024-29025 (unbounded form-field accumulation in HttpPostRequestDecoder); none shares this file, class or fix commit.

independent_corrections_accepted: The fix does not lower the default maximum. MAX_CLIENT_HELLO_LENGTH remains 0xFFFFFF, which getUnsignedMedium can never exceed, so the > comparison cannot fire on that default; moreover AbstractSniHandler() and SniHandler(Mapping) pass maxClientHelloLength=0, and the guard requires maxClientHelloLength != 0, so the default paths are entirely unchecked. Protection is opt-in via an explicit maximum in [1, 0xFFFFFF].

The entry point is confirmed as inherited: SniHandler -> AbstractSniHandler -> SslClientHelloHandler, and neither subclass overrides decode; a ~9-byte record declaring handshakeLength=0xFFFFFF reaches the allocation.
4.1.59 is in range: 535da17e is not an ancestor of 4.1.59 but is an ancestor of netty-4.1.94.Final (release commit da1a448d), and 4.1.94.Final is published on Maven Central.
Severity and CWEs confirmed from public records: CNA GitHub_M 6.5 MEDIUM, NVD Primary and Secondary 6.5 MEDIUM, GHSA MODERATE; CWE-400 (CNA/GHSA) and CWE-770 (NVD Primary/GHSA).
review.duplicate_check: The reviewer confirmed this is distinct from the prior netty entries using public records: CVE-2021-37136 (Bzip2Decoder, codec-compression), CVE-2021-37137 (SnappyFrameDecoder, codec-compression), CVE-2021-43797 (HTTP header-name CRLF, codec-http), CVE-2021-21295 (HTTP/2 request smuggling, codec-http2) and CVE-2024-29025 (HttpPostRequestDecoder form accumulation, codec-http). Different packages, mechanisms and fix commits.

limitations: Static verification only; no TLS server, socket, handshake or allocation was run and no memory exhaustion was attempted.

The advisory attributes the allocation to SniHandler, but the load-bearing code is the inherited SslClientHelloHandler.decode; the location row points there and SniHandler is recorded as the entry point.

The 4.1.94 fix does not lower the default maximum: MAX_CLIENT_HELLO_LENGTH remains 0xFFFFFF (a value getUnsignedMedium cannot exceed) and AbstractSniHandler()/SniHandler(Mapping) pass maxClientHelloLength=0, which disables the guard. Only applications that explicitly pass a maxClientHelloLength in [1, 0xFFFFFF] are protected; upgrading alone leaves the default allocation bound unchanged.
The issue is a resource-exhaustion DoS and depends on the application exposing SniHandler on a reachable TCP port without an idle timeout to release stalled handshakes.
Only one location row is recorded (SslClientHelloHandler.decode); the same allocation affects any subclass of SslClientHelloHandler, not only SniHandler.
The local mirror is shallow at the fetched tags; ancestry of the fix in 4.1.94.Final was checked with merge-base against fetched commits and the parent relationship of the release commit.
open_questions: Whether other 4.1.x or 4.0.x release lines received the same fix commit was not investigated; OSV names only the 4.1 branch commits.
The advisory treats 4.1.94 as the fixed release even though the default behaviour is unchanged; this dataset records the fix as present but opt-in rather than asserting a default reduction.
